What happens: Dave draws the seats, moves one player by hand, then follows the app's hints as players go out, until the last six sit at the final table. Turn on seat drawing You switch it on when you create the tournament. In New Tournament, under Tables: 1. Turn on Draw Seats. 2. Choose Seats per Table, from 2 to 10. Dave picks 6. 3. Choose Tables. With Auto, House Rules counts the players when you draw and opens as many tables as they need. Or pick a number from 1 to 8. This is the only place to turn it on. Once the tournament has started, you can't add seat drawing to it. The rest of New Tournament is in Setting Up a Tournament. Draw the seats Wait until the players are in. On the tournament screen, scroll down below Payouts to the Tables card. Until you draw, it says Seats aren’t drawn yet and has one button, Draw Seats. Live Tournament: Prize Pool $750, 15 entries, $75 house fee, 15 of 15 players left, 20,000 avg stack, Payouts 1st $375, 2nd $225, 3rd $150, and the Tables card at the bottom Tap Draw Seats. House Rules asks first and says what will happen: 15 players get random seats at 3 tables of 6. Late entries go to the shortest table. Tap Draw Seats again to confirm. Dave scrolls to the Tables card, taps Draw Seats, confirms, and the card lists Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3 Draw Seats? 15 players get random seats at 3 tables of 6. Late entries go to the shortest table. A Draw Seats button The players are split as evenly as possible. Fifteen players at three tables of 6 means 5 at each table. Seats inside a table are random. The Tables card now lists each table with how many seats are taken, 5 of 6. And in Still In, the list of players who are still playing, each player's row shows their table and seat under the name, like Table 2, Seat 5. The Tables card after the draw: 6 seats per table, Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3, each 5 of 6. Below it Still In: Ben Table 2, Seat 5, Chris Table 1, Seat 3, Dave Table 1, Seat 5 Still In with each player's table and seat: Grace Table 2, Seat 3, Hannah Table 3, Seat 2, Jenna Table 2, Seat 6 and so on A player who joins after the draw, with a late entry (someone who arrives after the start) or a re-entry, gets a random free seat at the table with the fewest players. See Entries, Re-Entries and Add-Ons. Show the seats to the players The fastest way to seat a room is to let everyone read their seat themselves. Tap the Tables card to open the Tables screen, then tap the Seating button at the top right, the one with a display icon, next to More. Seating fills the whole screen with big, easy-to-read numbers: each name with its table and seat. A switch at the top has two views: Names lists everyone in alphabetical order, Tables shows them table by table. Put the phone on the table or hold it up, and close it with X when you're done. Seating: Maple Street Game, 15 players at 3 tables, Names selected. Ben Table 2 Seat 5, Chris Table 1 Seat 3, Dave Table 1 Seat 5, Grace Table 2 Seat 3, and so on The Tables screen You can also reach the Tables screen from More (the three dots at the top right of the tournament) and Tables. It shows each table with its seats from 1 up. A seat with nobody in it says Open. A small D marks the seat with the dealer button, so the dealer at each table knows where to start. House Rules only shows the button, it doesn't deal or move it for you. Under the table's name you see how many seats are taken and where the button is, like 5 of 6 seats, button on 1. The Tables screen in List: Table 1, 5 of 6 seats, button on 1, with 1 Tyler and the D, 2 Nina, 3 Chris, 4 Leo, 5 Dave, 6 Open. Table 2: 1 Sam, 2 Open, 3 Grace with the D, 4 Kevin, 5 Ben, 6 Jenna List and Map at the top switch between two views of the same seats. Map draws each table as an oval with the players around it, the way they actually sit. The Tables screen in Map: Table 1 as an oval with Tyler at 6, Dave at 5, Leo at 4, Chris at 3, Nina at 2 and an open seat 1 with the D. Table 2 with Jenna, Sam, Ben, Kevin, Grace and an open seat 2 House Rules remembers which view you used last. Move a player Before the first hand, Tyler asks to move away from the air vent. Dave taps Tyler's row. The Move Tyler sheet opens: A switch at the top of the sheet has two choices: Open Seat lists the free seats at every table. Tap one and tap the checkmark at the top right. Swap With lists the other players. Pick one, tap the checkmark, and the two trade seats. The line under the switch says where the player sits now, Now at Table 1, Seat 1. Dave holds Tyler's row, chooses Move to Seat, picks Seat 6 under Table 1 and taps the checkmark. Tyler is now in seat 6 at Table 1 Move Tyler: Open Seat selected, Now at Table 1, Seat 1. Open seats Table 1 Seat 6 with a checkmark, Table 2 Seat 2, Table 3 Seat 1 If you hold a player's row instead of tapping it, a menu opens with Move to Seat, Swap With and Player Out. Move to Seat opens the same sheet as a tap. The menu on Tyler's row: Move to Seat, Swap With, Player Out The dealer button doesn't move with the player. After the move, Tyler's old seat 1 is open and still has the button. To move the button, hold any seat and choose Button Here. Table 1 after the move: 1 Open with the D, 2 Nina, 3 Chris, 4 Leo, 5 Dave, 6 Tyler More on the Tables screen More at the top right of the Tables screen has: Add Table opens one more empty table, when a second room or a spare table frees up. Break Table 3 closes the table with the highest number. Its players move to the shortest tables. It asks first. You can't pick another table to break. To keep Table 3 and close a different one, move its players yourself. Seats per Table changes how many seats each table has. You can't choose fewer seats than someone is already sitting in: Seats per Table 5 fails while a player sits in seat 6. Draw Seats Again gives everyone still in a new random seat. It asks first. Balance Tables appears only when the tables are uneven, and makes the move House Rules suggests, the same move as the hint below. The More menu on the Tables screen: Add Table, Break Table 3, Seats per Table, Draw Seats Again Follow the hints as players go out You record busts as usual, with Player Out. See When a Player Is Out. After each bust House Rules checks the tables. When it's time to change something, a hint appears at the top of the tournament screen, above the prize pool. Tapping the hint opens a small panel with a button. Tap that button to do what the hint says. To leave things as they are, tap anywhere else. There are three hints. If more than one applies, House Rules shows the most useful one: the final table first, then breaking a table, then balancing. Break a table Chris, Hannah and Ben go out. Twelve players are left: 4 at Table 3 and 8 at Tables 1 and 2. Tables 1 and 2 have 12 seats, so the 4 free seats there are enough for Table 3's players. The hint says Break Table 3: The other tables have room for the 4 players of Table 3. The hint above the prize pool: Break Table 3, The other tables have room for the 4 players of Table 3. Below it 12 of 15 players left Dave taps the hint, then Break Table 3. Each of Table 3's players gets a random free seat at the table with the fewest players. A message confirms how many players moved. Their new seats show in Still In and on the Tables screen, so Dave reads them out. The hint opened: Break Table 3, The other tables have room for the 4 players of Table 3, and a Break Table 3 button The app always breaks the table with the highest number. Balance the tables When one table has two or more players more than another, House Rules suggests moving one player from the fullest table to an open seat at the shortest one. It picks the player at random, and keeps the same suggestion until the seats change. Grace, Omar, Nina and Leo go out. Eight are left at two tables: 5 at Table 2 and 3 at Table 1. The hint says Balance the Tables: Move Priya from Table 2 to Table 1, Seat 2. The hint above the prize pool: Balance the Tables, Move Priya from Table 2 to Table 1, Seat 2. Below it 8 of 15 players left Tap the hint. Move Priya makes the move. Choose Another Player opens the Tables screen, where you tap the row of the player you'd rather move. The hint opened: Balance the Tables, Move Priya from Table 2 to Table 1, Seat 2, with Move Priya and Choose Another Player Once the tables are even, the hint goes away. The tournament after the move: no hint, Prize Pool $750, 8 of 15 players left Draw the final table Rosa and Kevin go out. Six players are left, and one table of 6 holds them all. The hint says Final Table: 6 players left. Everyone draws a new seat at the final table. The hint above the prize pool: Final Table, 6 players left. Everyone draws a new seat at the final table. Below it 6 of 15 players left Tap the hint, then Draw Final Table. The other tables close and the last six get new random seats at Table 1. The hint opened: Final Table, 6 players left. Everyone draws a new seat at the final table, and a Draw Final Table button The Tables card with Table 1, 6 of 6, and Still In: Dave Table 1, Seat 1, Jenna Seat 2, Marcus Seat 5, Priya Seat 4, Sam Seat 3, Tyler Seat 6 From here on there are no more table hints. The tournament goes on as usual until one player is left. Mistakes A player moved to the wrong seat: move them again from the Tables screen. Moves don't touch money or places. The draw came out badly, for example two rivals side by side: More, Draw Seats Again on the Tables screen. Everyone still in gets a new random seat. You'd rather not follow a hint: you don't have to. Ignore it, or move players yourself on the Tables screen. The hint stays until the tables are fixed. Good to know Seats change only when you draw, move, balance or break a table. Nobody moves on their own. Busted players lose their seat. Their seat shows as Open. If you set Tables to a number in New Tournament, the draw opens that many tables even if fewer would do. Seat drawing works with re-entry, add-ons and bounties the same way. Related Setting Up a Tournament Entries, Re-Entries and Add-Ons When a Player Is Out

title: When a Player Is Out
headings: The last bust ends the tournament
Undo the last bust after the end
text: When a player loses all their chips, they are out, or "bust". You record it in House Rules with Player Out. The app gives them their finishing place, updates the players left and the average stack, and when only one player is left, it ends the tournament and names the winner. The example tournament All the screenshots come from one tournament at the Maple Street Game. Dave, the host, records everything on his phone, so in this story you are Dave. Dave also plays, as many hosts do. The price: a $50 buy-in plus a $5 house fee, $55 an entry, for 20,000 chips. Re-entry is open until Level 4. How these are set is in Setting Up a Tournament. The players: Dave, Jenna, Marcus, Priya, Sam and Tyler. Everyone has paid except Sam, who owes $55. The prize pool is the six $50 buy-ins, $300, whether paid yet or not. The $5 house fees stay with the house. Auto, the default payout plan, pays two places for six players: $195 for 1st and $105 for 2nd. What happens: Priya goes out to Jenna. Dave records it, undoes it, and records it again. Then Sam, Dave and Tyler go out, and finally Marcus, so Jenna wins. At the end Dave tries Back In to see how a mistake is fixed. Record a bust There are two ways to start: Tap Player Out in the bar at the bottom of the tournament screen, between the cash box and +. Then tap Player and choose who went out. Or scroll down to Still In, the list of players who are still playing, and tap the player's row. The Player Out sheet opens with that player already chosen. Still In with Dave, Jenna, Marcus, Priya, Sam who owes $55, and Tyler. Payouts 1st 65% $195, 2nd 35% $105, 4 more out to the money 4 more out to the money under Payouts means four more players must go out before everyone left gets a prize. Priya loses a big hand to Jenna. Dave taps Priya's row. Dave taps Priya's row, the Player Out sheet opens, he picks Jenna under Knocked Out By, taps the checkmark, then taps Undo in the message The sheet has three parts: 1. Player: who went out, here Priya. 2. Re-Enter or Out in 6th. Tap one to choose it, and a check appears next to it. Out is chosen at the start. While re-entry is open, the player can buy back in instead of leaving. The note under it says when re-entry closes, Re-entry closes after Level 4. Out shows the place they finish in. With six players, the first one out is 6th. Re-entry is in Entries, Re-Entries and Add-Ons. 3. Knocked Out By: who won their last chips. It starts at Nobody. Tap it and pick a player if you want to keep track of knockouts. In a tournament without bounties it's optional. The line at the bottom says what the player gets: No prize, 5 players left. The Player Out sheet over the tournament: Player Priya, Re-Enter and Out in 6th with a checkmark, Re-entry closes after Level 4, Knocked Out By Nobody, No prize, 5 players left The Player Out sheet: Player Priya, Out in 6th checked, Knocked Out By Jenna, No prize, 5 players left Tap the checkmark button at the top right to save. A message at the bottom confirms it, Priya out in 6th. Priya is gone from Still In. A message at the bottom: Priya out in 6th, with Undo Undo a bust Picked the wrong player? Tap Undo in the message while it's still there. The player is back in Still In with their place cleared, as if nothing happened. Still In with Priya back: Dave, Jenna, Marcus, Priya, Sam, Tyler Dave records Priya's bust again, this time for real. Under Still In a new list appears, Out: each player who went out, with the time, who knocked them out, and their place. Still In with Dave, Jenna, Marcus, Sam and Tyler, and the start of the Out list below Once the message is gone, you can still undo the latest bust. Hold that player's row in Out and choose Back In. It does the same as Undo: the player goes back to Still In and their place is cleared. The menu on Priya's row in Out, Priya 12:58 PM, by Jenna, 6th, with Back In Only the latest bust can be undone. If Priya went out, then Sam, you bring Sam back first, then Priya. Nobody knocked them out Sam runs out of chips in a hand with three players, and nobody is sure whose chips finished him. Dave leaves Knocked Out By at Nobody and saves. Five players were left, so Sam finishes 5th and four remain. The Player Out sheet: Player Sam, Out in 5th checked, Re-entry closes after Level 4, Knocked Out By Nobody, No prize, 4 players left Sam still owes his $55. Going out doesn't change that. He pays before the end, and Dave records it in the cash box. See The Cash Box. The last bust ends the tournament Dave goes out 4th to Marcus, Tyler 3rd to Jenna. Two players are left, Jenna and Marcus, and both are in the money. From now on a Deal button also shows in the bottom bar, for when the last players agree to split the prize pool instead of playing on. See Making a Deal. Marcus goes all in and loses to Jenna. Dave records Marcus out in 2nd, knocked out by Jenna. The line at the bottom of the sheet now says what Marcus gets: Wins $105. Dave opens Player Out, picks Marcus and Jenna, saves, and the screen turns into Tournament Over with Jenna wins $195 The Player Out sheet: Player Marcus, Out in 2nd checked, Knocked Out By Jenna, Wins $105 Save, and the tournament is over. The message says Marcus out in 2nd and Jenna wins. If the blind timer runs for this tournament, it pauses at the last bust. Tournament Over: Ready to Settle, Jenna wins $195. Final Standings and a message: Marcus out in 2nd, Jenna wins, with Undo The tournament screen turns into Tournament Over: Ready to Settle is a card, not a button. It names the winner and the prize, Jenna wins $195, with the number of players, entries and the prize pool. Final Standings lists everyone by place, with what they won and paid. The number on the right is their result for the night: Jenna +$140 ($195 won minus $55 paid), Marcus +$50, everyone else −$55. Settle Up at the bottom opens the closing steps: you pay the prizes out of the cash box and record it, collect what's still owed, like Sam's $55, and close the tournament. The app records the money, it doesn't move it. See Prize Pool and Payouts. Tournament Over: Ready to Settle, Jenna wins $195, 6 players, 6 entries, pool $300. Final Standings: 1st Jenna won $195 paid $55 +$140, 2nd Marcus won $105 paid $55 +$50, 3rd Tyler, 4th Dave, 5th Sam owes $55, 6th Priya, each −$55. Settle Up at the bottom Undo the last bust after the end Say Dave recorded the wrong player as the last one out. Before Settle Up, hold Marcus's row in Final Standings and choose Back In. The menu on 2nd Marcus in Final Standings with Back In Marcus goes back to Still In next to Jenna, and the tournament is running again with 2 of 6 players left. Jenna isn't the winner anymore until the next bust. Now record the bust that really happened. Live Tournament again: Prize Pool $300, 6 entries, $30 house fee, 2 of 6 players left, 60,000 avg stack, 120,000 chips in play, Payouts In the money Good to know Places go down from the bottom: with six players, the first out is 6th, the next 5th, and so on. You never type a place. A player who re-enters doesn't get a place. They are back in with a new stack. See Entries, Re-Entries and Add-Ons. Knocked Out By counts knockouts in the club's statistics and in season points, if your season gives points for knockouts. See Season Points. In a bounty tournament you must pick who knocked the player out, up to two players, because the bounty goes to them. See Fixed Bounties and PKO. Going out doesn't touch money. Unpaid entries stay owed until the player pays. Related Entries, Re-Entries and Add-Ons Prize Pool and Payouts Making a Deal Tables and Seats

title: Prize Pool and Payouts
headings: How the places split the pool
Add your part when you close
text: The prize pool is the money the winners share. House Rules builds it from the buy-ins and add-ons, takes out any dealer tips, and tops it up to the guarantee if there is one. Then it splits the pool between the paid places, the payouts. This page explains where every dollar comes from, how to change the number of paid places and their shares, and what happens when the buy-ins don't reach the guarantee. The example tournament All the screenshots come from one tournament at the Maple Street Game. Dave, the host, runs it on his phone, so in this story you are Dave. The price: a $50 buy-in plus a $5 house fee, $55 an entry, no re-entry. The promise: Dave announced a $600 guarantee, a prize pool of at least $600 however many people come. Dealer tips: 3% of the buy-ins, for the friend who deals all night. What happened: only ten players came, all paid. Jenna won, Marcus came 2nd, Dave 3rd. Now Dave checks the payouts before he pays everyone. How the price, guarantee and tips are set is in Setting Up a Tournament. Where the money comes from The tournament is over and the screen shows Final Standings. Jenna wins $300, and the card at the top says the pool is $600, even though ten $50 buy-ins make only $500. The difference is the guarantee. The numbers on the right are each player's result, prize minus what they paid. Dave's +$65 doesn't count the money he adds for the guarantee, see below. Tournament Over: Ready to Settle, Jenna wins $300, 10 players, 10 entries, pool $600. Final Standings: 1st Jenna won $300 paid $55 +$245, 2nd Marcus won $180 +$125, 3rd Dave won $120 +$65, 4th Priya, 5th Tyler, 6th Sam paid $55 −$55. $550 and Settle Up at the bottom To see the whole picture, open Payouts. From top to bottom it has Places Paid and Round To, the Places, then Guarantee and Dealer Tips, and last Where the Money Goes. To open it: during the tournament tap the Payouts card, or at any time tap More (the three dots at the top right) and choose Payouts. Scroll down to Where the Money Goes. Payouts: Guarantee $600, Dealer Tips Percent, Tips 3%. Where the Money Goes: 10 entries × $50 $500, Dealer Tips 3% −$15, Guarantee $600 guaranteed +$115, Prize Pool $600, House Fee 10 × $5 $50 goes to the overlay, From You $65 Read it from the top: 10 entries × $50, $500: the buy-ins, without the house fee. Dealer Tips 3%, −$15: the tips come off the top. The $15 stays in the cash box for the dealer. Guarantee, +$115: what's missing to reach $600. This gap is called the overlay. Prize Pool, $600: what the places share. House Fee 10 × $5, $50: the house fee is the host's money, here Dave's. It was never part of the $500, and it pays the overlay first. From You, $65: the rest of the overlay, $115 − $50, comes out of Dave's own pocket. So the guarantee cost Dave his $50 house fee and $65 more. Tips come off before the guarantee is checked, so they make the overlay bigger. With thirteen players, $650 of buy-ins minus $19.50 in tips would clear $600 on their own, and the Guarantee line would disappear. Add-ons count toward the pool the same way as buy-ins. Re-entries count as entries. How the places split the pool At the top of Payouts: Places Paid is how many players get a prize. Auto (3) means House Rules picks the number from the entries: Auto pays 1 place up to 4 entries, 2 up to 7, 3 up to 15, 4 up to 24, then 5. Ten entries pay three places. Round To keeps the prizes in round numbers: $0.01, $1, $5 or $10. Places lists each place with its share and its prize. Here 1st gets 50%, $300, 2nd 30%, $180, and 3rd 20%, $120. Payouts: Places Paid Auto (3), Round To $1. Auto pays 1 place up to 4 entries, 2 up to 7, 3 up to 15, 4 up to 24, then 5. Places: 1st 50% $300, 2nd 30% $180, 3rd 20% $120. Percents add up to 100%. Rounding leftovers go to 1st place Pay more places Priya finished 4th and the table thinks she deserves her money back. Dave taps Places Paid and picks 4. Dave taps Places Paid, picks 4, and the places change to 45% $270, 27% $162, 17% $102, 11% $66. Then he taps 1st place's share and the keys open with 45 The Places Paid menu: Auto (3) checked, then 1 to 10 House Rules splits the pool between four places with its standard shares: 45%, 27%, 17% and 11%. That's $270, $162, $102 and $66, still $600 in all. Payouts with Places Paid 4: 1st 45% $270, 2nd 27% $162, 3rd 17% $102, 4th 11% $66 Change a share The shares are buttons. Tap one, for example 1st place's 45%, and type the new share on the keys. Tap the checkmark to set it. The keys over Payouts: 1st Place, % 45, Share of the prize pool The shares must add up to exactly 100%. While they don't, the prizes disappear from the list and the note under the places says how far off you are, for example Percents add up to 95%. Make it 100% to save them. Change another share until the total is 100%, and the new split saves. To go back to the standard split, choose Auto in Places Paid. Auto sets both the number of places and their shares, so here it goes back to three places. Rounding The Round To menu: $0.01, $1 checked, $5, $10 Every place except 1st rounds down to the Round To amount, and whatever is left over goes to 1st. For example, with four places and Round To $10, 2nd gets $160 instead of $162, 3rd $100, 4th $60, and 1st gets the rest, $280. Pick $0.01 to pay exact amounts. Guarantee and dealer tips Below the places are the Guarantee, Dealer Tips and the tips amount. You can change them during the tournament and after it, until you settle. Guarantee: tap the amount and type a new one. Zero means no guarantee. Dealer Tips: Off for no tips, Percent for a share of the buy-ins, up to 20%, or Amount for a fixed sum for the whole tournament. Tips come out of the prize pool and stay in the cash box for the dealer. Two limits protect money that has already moved. You can't lower the guarantee so far that the money you already added for it is more than it needs: House Rules says Delete the money you added for the guarantee from the cash box first. And you can't lower the tips below what you've already paid the dealer from the cash box: Delete the tips paid from the cash box first. In both cases the settings stay as they were. While a deal stands, the guarantee and tips can only be viewed. The note under them sums up the rule: The house fee covers a guarantee shortfall first, you add the rest. Dealer tips come off the top and go to the cash box for the dealer. Add your part when you close When the guarantee needs money from you, the tournament can't be settled until you put it in the cash box. Dave taps Settle Up on the Tournament Over screen. Close Tournament opens with its steps: Places checks everyone has a place, House Fee settles the guarantee, Expenses is for costs like food, Collect gets in money still owed, and Settle Up pays the prizes. Here House Fee says Add $65 for the guarantee. The steps are explained in Close Session, Step by Step. Close Tournament: Steps. Places, Everyone has a place, checked. House Fee, Add $65 for the guarantee. Expenses, Not needed. Collect, Everyone has paid, checked. Settle Up, Who pays whom. An Add $65 button at the bottom Dave puts $65 of his own cash into the box with the rest of the money, then taps Add $65 so the app records it. House Rules never moves real money, it only keeps track. The message says Added $65 for the guarantee, the step is checked, and From Cash Box lists the prizes to pay: Jenna $300, Marcus $180 and, further down the list, Dave $120. Dave taps Add $65, the House Fee step gets a check, and From Cash Box lists Jenna $300 and Marcus $180 Close Tournament: House Fee, You added $65 for the guarantee, checked. Settle Up, 0 of 3 marked. From Cash Box, 0 of 3: Jenna $300, Marcus $180. A message: Added $65 for the guarantee. Close for Now at the bottom Check the sums: the box held $550 from ten $55 entries. With Dave's $65 it holds $615. Out of that go the $600 in prizes and the $15 dealer tips. Nothing is left, because the house fee went to the overlay. Counting his $65, Dave's real result for the night is $120 won minus $55 paid minus $65 added, so he breaks even. Paying the prizes and marking them done is in Close Session, Step by Step. Good to know Rounding leftovers always go to 1st place, so the prizes add up to the whole pool. Auto pays at most five places. For more, pick the number yourself, up to 10. After a deal, Places Paid and the shares are locked, and the deal amounts are paid instead. See Making a Deal. Bounties are paid on top of the prizes and aren't part of the prize pool. See Fixed Bounties and PKO. The house fee belongs to the house. When there's no overlay to cover, it's yours to keep. Related Setting Up a Tournament When a Player Is Out Making a Deal Close Session, Step by Step

title: Making a Deal
headings: When you can make a deal
text: Late at night, with the last few players all in the money, someone often says: "Let's chop it." Instead of playing on until one player has every chip, the players agree to split the prizes that are left. That's a deal. House Rules does the math from the chip counts, shows the amounts for three ways of splitting, and pays the deal instead of the places. The example tournament All the screenshots come from one tournament at the Maple Street Game. Dave, the host, runs it on his phone, so in this story you are Dave. The price: a $50 buy-in plus a $5 house fee, no re-entry. Ten players, all paid, make a $500 prize pool. The payouts: Auto pays three places: $250 for 1st, $150 for 2nd, $100 for 3rd. How these are counted is in Prize Pool and Payouts. The final three: Jenna, Marcus and Priya, all in the money. Jenna has 95,000 chips, Marcus 65,000, Priya 40,000. It's almost 1 a.m. and everyone has work tomorrow. What happens: they look at the three ways to split, take ICM, and leave $40 to play for. Then they play on: Priya goes out, then Marcus, and Jenna wins the $40. When you can make a deal Once everyone left is in the money, here three players for three paid places, a Deal button appears in the bar at the bottom of the tournament. With four buttons the bar has no room for words and shows icons only. Deal is the third icon, a round dial, between Player Out and +. Live Tournament: Prize Pool $500, 10 entries, $50 house fee, 3 of 10 players left, 66,666 avg stack, 200,000 chips in play. Payouts In the money: 1st 50% $250, 2nd 30% $150, 3rd 20% $100. The bottom bar shows four icons: cash box, Player Out, Deal and + You can also open it from More (the three dots at the top right) and Make a Deal. The menu item shows up earlier than the button: as soon as ten players or fewer are left and there are prizes still to pay, even before everyone is in the money. Enter the stacks Dave taps Deal. The Make a Deal sheet opens with the players still in under Stacks. Ask each player to count their chips, then tap the box next to their name and type the count on the keys. Dave taps the box next to Jenna, types 95000, then Marcus 65000 and Priya 40000. The Deal amounts fill in The keys over Make a Deal: Jenna, Chips 95,000 The line under the stacks checks the count: 200,000 of 200,000 chips in play. If it doesn't match, someone miscounted, or a stack was typed wrong. Recount before you go on. Make a Deal: Stacks Jenna 95,000, Marcus 65,000, Priya 40,000, 200,000 of 200,000 chips in play. Even, Chips and ICM with ICM selected. Deal $500: Jenna 1st pays $250 $190, Marcus 2nd pays $150 $167, Priya 3rd pays $100 $143 Under Deal, each player's row shows the prize their place would pay without a deal, like 1st pays $250, and on the right what they get from the deal. Pick how to split The switch above the Deal section has three ways to split the $500 left: Even: everyone gets the same. Rounding leftovers go to the chip leader. Chips: everyone first gets the smallest prize still to be paid, here 3rd place's $100. The other $200 is split in proportion to the chips. ICM: by each player's chances to finish in every place, worked out from the chip counts. This is the usual choice in poker rooms, and the one House Rules starts with. For Dave's table: Even: Jenna $168, Marcus $166, Priya $166. Chips: Jenna $195, Marcus $165, Priya $140. ICM: Jenna $190, Marcus $167, Priya $143. Make a Deal with Even: Marcus $166, Priya $166. Everyone gets the same. Rounding leftovers go to the chip leader Make a Deal with Chips: Marcus $165, Priya $140. Everyone gets the last place's prize, the rest goes by chip count Make a Deal with ICM: Marcus $167, Priya $143. By each player's chances to finish in every place, from the chip counts Chips pays the leader the most, because it treats every chip as worth the same. ICM reasons that Jenna's extra chips don't guarantee her 1st, while even Priya's short stack still has a real chance of 2nd, so it pays the short stacks a little more. Even is for friends who just want to go home. The three players agree on ICM. Leave some to play for Often players split most of the money but keep a bit to play for, so the game still has a winner. Tap Leave to Play For and type the amount. It can be up to the gap between 1st and 2nd place, here $100, so the player who finishes 2nd never gets less than 2nd place would pay. The keys over Make a Deal: Leave to Play For $40, Up to $100, the gap between 1st and 2nd place Dave types $40. Now the ICM split works on the $460 left, and the note says $40 goes to the winner. Keep playing and mark players out as usual. Jenna gets $171, Marcus $154, Priya $135, $460 in all. Whoever wins also gets the $40 on top. Make a Deal: Marcus 2nd pays $150 $154, Priya 3rd pays $100 $135. Leave to Play For $40. $40 goes to the winner. Keep playing and mark players out as usual If you leave nothing to play for, the deal ends the tournament right away: the screen turns into Tournament Over, and places go by chip count, the biggest stack 1st. Make the deal To save the deal, tap the checkmark button at the top right of the sheet. Its name is Make Deal. The tournament screen now shows a Deal card in place of Payouts: the ICM deal with each player's amount, and Play For, to the winner, $40. Live Tournament after the deal: Prize Pool $500, 3 of 10 players left. Deal, ICM deal: Jenna $171, Marcus $154, Priya $135, Play For, to the winner $40 Payouts now opens with the deal at the top. The places below are marked Places Before the Deal, and Places Paid and percents are locked while the deal stands. Payouts: Deal, ICM deal $500: Jenna 95,000 chips $171, Marcus 65,000 chips $154, Priya 40,000 chips $135, Play For, to the winner $40, and Cancel Deal. The winner also gets the amount left to play for. Places Paid Auto (3) and Round To $1 locked. Places Before the Deal Play for the rest The three play on for the $40. Priya goes out first. Dave records it with Player Out as usual. The note under the sheet says what she gets: Gets $135 from the deal. Player Out: Player Priya, Knocked Out By Nobody, Gets $135 from the deal Then Marcus goes out, and Jenna wins. After a deal, the order players go out in doesn't change anyone's amount. Only the winner gets the $40. Jenna's prize is her $171 plus the $40: Jenna wins $211. Tournament Over: Ready to Settle, Jenna wins $211, 10 players, 10 entries, pool $500. Final Standings: 1st Jenna deal $211 paid $55 +$156, 2nd Marcus deal $154 paid $55 +$99, 3rd Priya deal $135 paid $55 +$80, 4th Dave paid $55 −$55 Each row in Final Standings says deal instead of won. Paid is the $55 each player paid, buy-in plus house fee. The seven players who went out before the deal are listed below Priya, from 4th to 10th. From here you settle as usual with Settle Up. See Prize Pool and Payouts. Cancel a deal Changed your mind, or typed a stack wrong? Tap More and Cancel Deal, or Cancel Deal at the top of Payouts. House Rules asks first. Everyone in the deal goes back in to play, even a player who went out after the deal, and payouts go back to places. Then make the deal again with the right numbers. The tournament's More menu after a deal: Payouts, House Rules, Blind Timer, Cancel Deal, Close Tournament, Share Tournament, Hand Over Tournament, Delete Tournament Good to know A deal splits only what's still to be paid. Prizes of players already out don't change. Bounties stay outside the deal. Each player keeps the bounties they've won. See Fixed Bounties and PKO. A deal works for 2 to 10 players. The deal is a record of what the players agreed. If they want different amounts, for example to round them, change the stacks or the method until the numbers match what they said. Related Prize Pool and Payouts When a Player Is Out Fixed Bounties and PKO

title: Fixed Bounties and PKO
headings: A re-entry brings a new bounty
Halves that don't split to the dollar
The winner keeps their own bounty
text: In a bounty tournament every player has a price on their head. Each entry pays a bounty on top of the buy-in, and whoever knocks that player out collects it. It gives everyone a reason to play for knockouts, not only for the top places. House Rules has two kinds: Fixed: the player who knocks someone out gets the whole bounty in cash. Progressive, also called PKO (progressive knockout): they get half of that player's bounty in cash, and the other half is added to their own bounty. The more players you knock out, the bigger your own bounty grows, and the more you're worth to whoever knocks you out. Bounties are separate from the prize pool. The places share the buy-ins, the knockers share the bounties, and House Rules keeps track of both and pays them together at the end. The example tournament All the screenshots come from the Maple Street Game's first PKO. Dave is the host and also plays. He runs the tournament on his phone, so in this story you are Dave. The price: a $40 buy-in, a $20 progressive bounty and a $5 house fee: $65 an entry. Re-entry is open until Level 4: a player who goes out can pay $65 again for a new stack and a new bounty. The players: eight, all paid. Eight entries of $65 bring $520 into the cash box: $320 for the prize pool, $160 for bounties and $40 of house fees. What happens: Jenna knocks out Sam. Marcus knocks out Rosa, who re-enters. Tyler and Priya knock out Kevin together. Then the rest go out one by one, and Jenna wins. Turn on bounties You set bounties when you create the tournament. In New Tournament, next to the buy-in: 1. Set Bounty to Fixed or Progressive. Dave picks Progressive. 2. Set the Bounty Amount, here $20. Each entry then pays the buy-in, the bounty and the house fee. The rest of New Tournament is in Setting Up a Tournament. The tournament with bounties The Prize Pool card now also shows the bounties: 8 entries, $160 in bounties, $40 house fee. One of the tiles counts the bounties paid out so far, $0 of $160 bounties won. Live Tournament: Prize Pool $320, 8 entries, $160 in bounties, $40 house fee. Tiles: 8 of 8 players left, 20,000 avg stack, $0 of $160 bounties won, 0:30 running. Payouts 1st 50% $160, 2nd 30% $96, 3rd 20% $64. $520 at the bottom In Still In, the list of players who are still playing, each row shows the player's current bounty next to a target symbol, $20 for everyone at the start. Still In: Dave, Jenna, Kevin, Marcus, Priya, Rosa, Sam and Tyler, each with a $20 bounty Knock someone out Jenna wins a big pot and Sam is out. Dave taps Player Out in the bar at the bottom of the tournament screen. In the sheet that opens he taps Player and picks Sam, then taps the Knocked Out By row and picks Jenna. How busts work in general is in When a Player Is Out. In a bounty tournament you must pick who knocked the player out, because the bounty goes to them. Until you do, you can't save. Dave opens Player Out, picks Sam, picks Jenna under Knocked Out By, and saves. The message says Sam out in 8th, Jenna +$10 Under the knocker, House Rules spells out the bounty: Jenna gets $10. Half of Sam’s $20 bounty. Jenna’s bounty grows to $30. Player Out: Player Sam, Out in 8th, Knocked Out By Jenna. Jenna gets $10. Half of Sam's $20 bounty. Jenna's bounty grows to $30. Two players knocked Sam out? Pick both to split it. No prize, 7 players left Tap the checkmark at the top right of the sheet to save. A message at the bottom of the screen says Sam out in 8th and Jenna +$10, with an Undo button. The tile now reads $10 of $160 bounties won. Live Tournament: 7 of 8 players left, $10 of $160 bounties won. A message: Sam out in 8th, Jenna +$10, with Undo With a Fixed bounty, Jenna would get all $20 in cash, and her own bounty would stay $20. A re-entry brings a new bounty Marcus knocks out Rosa. Re-entry is still open, so Rosa buys back in. In the Player Out sheet Dave picks Rosa, taps Re-Enter instead of Out, and picks Marcus under Knocked Out By. Marcus still collects Rosa's bounty: Marcus gets $10. Half of Rosa’s $20 bounty. Marcus’s bounty grows to $30. Rosa pays $65 again, and the note says what she gets: New stack of 20,000 and a new $20 bounty, $65 to the cash box. Player Out: Player Rosa, Re-Enter checked, Re-entry closes after Level 4. Knocked Out By Marcus: Marcus gets $10. Half of Rosa's $20 bounty. Marcus's bounty grows to $30. Paid on. New stack of 20,000 and a new $20 bounty, $65 to the cash box Rosa's second $65 adds $40 to the prize pool, $20 to the bounties and $5 to the house fee. The pool is now $360 and the bounties $180. Two players knock someone out Kevin goes all in against Tyler and Priya and loses to both: each of them wins part of the pot. They split his bounty. Under Knocked Out By, pick both players. You can pick up to two. A third tap replaces the second. Knocked Out By: Search Players, then Dave, Jenna, Marcus, Priya with a checkmark, Rosa, Tyler with a checkmark. Pick up to two. A third tap swaps the second The split is even: Tyler gets $5 and Priya gets $5. Half of Kevin’s $20 bounty, split. Tyler’s bounty grows to $25. Priya’s bounty grows to $25. Player Out: Player Kevin, Out in 7th, Knocked Out By Tyler and Priya. Tyler gets $5 and Priya gets $5. Half of Kevin's $20 bounty, split. Tyler's bounty grows to $25. Priya's bounty grows to $25. No prize, 6 players left When an amount can't be split evenly to the dollar, the first player you picked gets the extra dollar. Follow the bounties After three knockouts the Prize Pool card shows 9 entries, $180 in bounties, $45 house fee and $30 of $180 bounties won. Live Tournament: Prize Pool $360, 9 entries, $180 in bounties, $45 house fee. 6 of 8 players left, 30,000 avg stack, $30 of $180 bounties won. Payouts 1st $180, 2nd $108, 3rd $72 In Still In, each player's row says how many players they've knocked out and how much they've won, and the bounty on their head now: Jenna 1 knockout, won $10, with a $30 bounty. Rosa's row says 2 entries: she's on her second stack, with a new $20 bounty. Still In: Dave $20, Jenna 1 knockout, won $10, $30. Marcus 1 knockout, won $10, $30. Priya 1 knockout, won $5, $25. Rosa 2 entries, $20. Tyler 1 knockout, won $5, $25. Out: Sam, by Jenna, 8th Halves that don't split to the dollar Later Marcus knocks out Tyler, whose bounty is $25. Half of $25 is $12.50. House Rules rounds the cash part down to the tournament's Round To step, here $1, and adds the rest to the knocker's bounty: Marcus gets $12 in cash, and the other $13 is added to his bounty, which grows from $30 to $43. The winner keeps their own bounty Dave, Tyler, Priya and Rosa go out. Jenna knocks out Dave, Priya and Rosa, Marcus knocks out Tyler. At the end it's Jenna against Marcus, and Jenna wins: Jenna gets $21. Half of Marcus’s $43 bounty. Jenna’s bounty grows to $85. The line at the bottom says Marcus's prize for 2nd: Wins $108. Player Out: Player Marcus, Out in 2nd, Knocked Out By Jenna. Jenna gets $21. Half of Marcus's $43 bounty. Jenna's bounty grows to $85. Wins $108 Nobody knocks out the winner, so Jenna keeps the $85 on her own head. That's why progressive bounties reward the winner twice: 1st place, and the biggest bounty in the room. The Tournament Over card says Jenna wins $180, plus $148 in bounties. Her $148 is the $63 she collected in cash plus her own $85 bounty. The cash came from five knockouts: Sam $10, Dave $10, Priya $12 (half of $25), Rosa $10 and Marcus $21. Tournament Over: Ready to Settle, Jenna wins $180, plus $148 in bounties, 8 players, 9 entries. Final Standings: 1st Jenna won $180, bounties $148, paid $65, +$263. 2nd Marcus won $108, bounties $22, paid $65, +$65. 3rd Rosa won $72, paid $130, −$58. 4th Priya bounties $5, paid $65, −$60. 5th Tyler bounties $5, paid $65, −$60. 6th Dave paid $65, −$65 Final Standings shows each player's prize, bounties and what they paid. Rosa paid $130 for two entries, so her $72 for 3rd still leaves her −$58. Priya and Tyler each won $5 in bounties. Final Standings: 1st Jenna +$263, 2nd Marcus +$65, 3rd Rosa −$58, 4th Priya −$60, 5th Tyler −$60, 6th Dave −$65, 7th Kevin paid $65 −$65, 8th Sam paid $65 −$65 Settle up Tap Settle Up. From Cash Box pays each player their prize and bounties in one amount: Jenna $328 ($180 prize and $148 bounties), Marcus $130 ($108 and $22), Rosa $72, Tyler $5 and Priya $5. Close Tournament: Steps Places, Everyone has a place. House Fee, $45 to the cash box. Rakeback, Not distributed. Kept by House $45. Expenses, Not needed. Collect, Everyone has paid. Settle Up, 0 of 5 marked. From Cash Box: Jenna, Prize +$180, bounties +$148, $328 From Cash Box, 0 of 5: Jenna Prize +$180, bounties +$148, $328. Marcus Prize +$108, bounties +$22, $130. Rosa $72. Tyler $5. Priya $5 Check the box: nine entries of $65 brought in $585. Out go $360 in prizes and $180 in bounties, $540 in all. What's left, $45, is the house fee. The closing steps are in Close Session, Step by Step. Mistakes Wrong knocker, right after saving: tap Undo in the message, then record the bust again. The bounty goes back to where it was. Wrong knocker, later: only the latest bust can be undone. Scroll down to the Out list under Still In, hold the last player's row and choose Back In, then fix the busts in order. See When a Player Is Out. Good to know Bounties aren't part of the prize pool, and the guarantee and dealer tips don't touch them. A deal doesn't touch bounties either. Each player keeps the bounties they've won, and players in the deal keep their own heads. See Making a Deal. Every re-entry brings a new bounty. The grown bounty from the player's earlier stack went to whoever knocked them out. Season points can count knockouts. See Season Points. Related Setting Up a Tournament When a Player Is Out Prize Pool and Payouts Making a Deal

title: How Season Points Work
headings: The season on the club screen
text: A season turns your club's tournaments into a league. Every finish scores points, the points add up across the season, and the club sees a table of who's ahead. House Rules takes each player's finishing place from every tournament you ran in the app and turns it into points. You never type a point yourself. This page shows how to start a season, read the standings, and choose how points are scored. The example club All the screenshots come from the Maple Street Game. Dave is the host and also plays. He runs the club on his phone, so in this story you are Dave. The tournaments: five since late October, all with a $50 buy-in plus a $5 house fee, seven or eight players each. All five are settled. The winners: Marcus won three, Jenna one, and Dave won the latest, on Sunday, November 22. What happens: the players want to know who had the best autumn. Dave starts the 2026 Season, looks at the standings, compares the two ways to score, and opens the latest tournament to see its points. Start a season Open your club and tap More, the three dots at the top right, then New Season. Dave opens More in the Maple Street Game, taps New Season, keeps the name 2026 Season, taps the checkmark, and the season opens with Dave leads by 4 points The club's More menu: Rename, Plan Game, All Games, New Season, Color, Hide House Rules A name box opens with 2026 Season already typed. Keep it or type your own. The note under it says what you get: the season runs from Jan 1 to Dec 31 of this year, and scores 10, 7, 5, 3, 2 points for the top five places and 1 for playing. You can change all of that later, for example shorter dates for a fall league. Tap the checkmark. The name box over the club screen: 2026 Season, with the note Jan 1 – Dec 31, points 10, 7, 5, 3, 2 and 1 for playing. Change them in Points Rules The season counts every tournament the club has finished within its dates, including those played before you created it. Dave's five autumn tournaments are all in 2026, so they score at once. Read the standings The season screen opens right away. At the top is the headline, Dave leads by 4 points, and how much the season covers: 5 tournaments, 8 players, the eight different people who played at least once. 2026 Season, Maple Street Game, Jan 1 – Dec 31. Dave leads by 4 points, 5 tournaments, 8 players. Standings: 1 Dave 5 played, 1 win, 41 pts. 2 Marcus 4 played, 3 wins, 37 pts. 3 Jenna 5 played, 1 win, 33 pts. 4 Tyler 22 pts. 5 Priya 20 pts. 6 Sam 9 pts. 7 Kevin 7 pts. 8 Rosa 4 pts Standings lists every player who played at least one tournament, with how many they played and won, and their points. Dave played all five and finished 2nd three times. Here is how his 41 adds up with the default points: 2nd place, three times: 7 + 7 + 7 = 21 3rd place once: 5 1st place once: 10 1 point for playing, five times: 5 In all: 21 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 41 Marcus won three times, 11 points each with the point for playing, and finished 4th in the latest tournament, 3 + 1 = 4. That's 37. He missed one night, and a missed night scores nothing, so Dave is 4 points ahead. If a player missing nights shouldn't fall behind like Marcus did, count only each player's best results. See Counting Only the Best Results. Below the standings, Tournaments lists the season's tournaments, newest first, with the number of players and the winner. Tap one to open it. The season screen scrolled down: Standings 4 to 8, then Tournaments: Sun, Nov 22, 8 players, Dave won. Tue, Nov 17, 8 players, Marcus won. Tue, Nov 10, 7 players, Jenna won. Tue, Nov 3, 7 players, Marcus won. Tue, Oct 27, 8 players, Marcus won To send the table to your players, tap the share button at the top right, the square with an arrow, left of More. Your phone's share sheet opens, so you can send it to a group chat or any other app. It has the places and points as text, with no money. Choose how points are scored On the season screen, tap More, the three dots at the top right, and Points Rules. The season's More menu: Points Rules, Rename Season, Season Dates, End Season, Delete Season The switch at the top picks one of two ways to score a finish: By Place or By Field. Tap one to see its settings. The checkmark at the top right keeps your changes, the X at the top left throws them away. By Place By Place is the default. You set the points for each place yourself under Points for Places: here 10 for 1st, 7 for 2nd, 5 for 3rd, 3 for 4th and 2 for 5th. Tap a number, type the new points on the keys that slide up, and tap their checkmark. Add Place adds the next place, up to 10. Places further down score nothing for the place itself. Points Rules with By Place: Points for Places, 1st Place 10, 2nd Place 7, 3rd Place 5, 4th Place 3, 5th Place 2, Add Place. Places further down score nothing for the place itself. For Playing 1. Best Results Count All By Place suits a club where about the same number of people come every time. A win is worth the same whether seven or eight players came. By Field By Field gives a point for every player you outlast, plus one. In a tournament of 12 players, 1st gets 12 and last gets 1. The point for playing is added on top. So a bigger tournament is worth more, and every place scores something. Points Rules with By Field: A point for every player you outlast, plus one: 1st of 12 players gets 12, last gets 1. For Playing 1. Best Results Count All For Dave's club, By Field would change the order behind him. Dave would have 38 points: 8 for 2nd of 8 players, 7 for 2nd of 7, 6 for 3rd of 7, 8 for 2nd of 8 and 9 for 1st of 8, each with the point for playing. Jenna would have 34 and Marcus 32: Jenna's five steady finishes would count for more than Marcus's wins in four tournaments. Dave only looks and taps the X, so nothing changes. Points for everyone Under the places, the same in both ways of scoring: For Playing: points for every tournament a player plays, to reward showing up. The default is 1. Per Knockout: points for every player a player knocks out. The row is hidden until your club has played a bounty tournament, where every knockout is recorded. See Fixed Bounties and PKO. Best Results Count: how many of each player's tournaments count. All counts every one. See Counting Only the Best Results. House Rules counts the points again from the places every time you open the season. So a change in Points Rules recounts the whole season at once, past tournaments too. Points in each tournament Every tournament in the season shows its points. Dave opens the latest one, from Tournaments on the season screen. In Final Standings, each player's row now ends with their points: Dave 11 pts for 1st (10 for the place and 1 for playing), Jenna 8, Priya 6, Marcus 4, Tyler 3, and 1 pt each for Kevin, Sam and Rosa, who finished below 5th. Tournament Ended, Dave wins $200, 8 players, 8 entries, pool $400. Final Standings: 1st Dave won $200, paid $55, 11 pts, +$145. 2nd Jenna won $120, paid $55, 8 pts. 3rd Priya won $80, paid $55, 6 pts. 4th Marcus paid $55, 4 pts. 5th Tyler 3 pts. 6th Kevin, 7th Sam and 8th Rosa 1 pt each The season on the club screen Back on the club screen, a 2026 Season card now shows the top three, with 5 tournaments at the top right. Tap the card to open the season. Maple Street Game club screen with a 2026 Season card: 5 tournaments, 1 Dave 41 pts, 2 Marcus 37 pts, 3 Jenna 33 pts What scores and what doesn't Only the club's tournaments score. Cash games don't. A tournament scores once it's over: the last player is out or a deal ends it. You don't have to finish Settle Up first. A tournament still running doesn't count yet. See When a Player Is Out. It must start within the season's dates. To change them, tap More and Season Dates on the season screen. A player who re-enters still finishes in one place, so a tournament is one result for them. Good to know Ties in the standings go to more wins, then to the better place in the latest tournament. The headline says leads on wins when the top two have the same points. Renaming a season or changing its dates never changes any tournament. To end or delete a season, tap More on the season screen. Both are explained in Counting Only the Best Results. Related Counting Only the Best Results Fixed Bounties and PKO When a Player Is Out

title: Counting Only the Best Results
text: In a long season, some players can't come every time. If every tournament counts, every night adds points, so a player who shows up every time can collect more than a better player who missed a night. Best Results Count fixes that: only each player's highest-scoring tournaments add up. Their lower-scoring ones are dropped, and a missed night just means one fewer result to choose from. This page also covers ties, sharing the standings, the season's dates, and ending or deleting a season. The example club The story picks up where How Season Points Work left off. Dave is the host of the Maple Street Game and also plays, so in this story you are Dave. The season: the 2026 Season, running all of 2026. The club has played five tournaments since late October, all settled and the default points: 10, 7, 5, 3, 2 for the top five places and 1 for playing. The standings: Dave leads with 41 points. He played all five tournaments. Marcus has 37: he won three of the four he played, but missed one night. What happens: the club agrees that missing one night shouldn't cost Marcus the lead. Dave sets Best Results Count to 4, shares the new standings, and looks at the season's dates and how to end it. 2026 Season: Dave leads by 4 points, 5 tournaments, 8 players. Standings: 1 Dave 5 played, 1 win, 41 pts. 2 Marcus 4 played, 3 wins, 37 pts. 3 Jenna 33 pts. 4 Tyler 22 pts. 5 Priya 20 pts. 6 Sam 9 pts. 7 Kevin 7 pts. 8 Rosa 4 pts Count only the best results Open your club and tap the season card, here 2026 Season. On the season screen, tap More, the three dots at the top right, then Points Rules. At the bottom, tap Best Results Count and pick a number. All counts every tournament. The other choices are 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Dave opens More, Points Rules, taps Best Results Count, picks 4, taps the checkmark, and the season now says Marcus leads by 2 points Points Rules with the Best Results Count menu open: All checked, then 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 Dave picks 4, and the row now reads Best Results Count 4. Tap the checkmark at the top right of Points Rules to save. Nothing changes until you do. The X at the top left closes without saving. Points Rules: By Place, 1st Place 10, 2nd 7, 3rd 5, 4th 3, 5th 2, For Playing 1, Best Results Count 4. Only a player's best tournaments count when you set Best Results Count. Ties go to more wins, then the better place in the latest tournament The new standings The season recounts at once. The headline now says Marcus leads by 2 points, and the line under it adds best 4 count. 2026 Season: Marcus leads by 2 points, 5 tournaments, 8 players, best 4 count. Standings: 1 Marcus 4 played, 3 wins, 37 pts. 2 Dave 5 played, 1 win, 35 pts. 3 Jenna 29 pts. 4 Tyler 21 pts. 5 Priya 19 pts. 6 Sam 8 pts. 7 Kevin 6 pts. 8 Rosa 4 pts Here's why, with the default points plus 1 for playing: Marcus played only four tournaments, so all four still count: 11 + 11 + 11 for his three wins (10 plus 1 each) and 4 for a 4th place (3 plus 1). That's 37, the same as before. Dave played five. His results were 11 for his win, 8 for each of his three 2nd places (7 plus 1), and 6 for his 3rd place (5 plus 1), 41 in all. The best four are 11 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 35. His weakest result, the 6, no longer counts. Jenna also loses her weakest result, a 4 for 4th place: 33 becomes 29. Tyler, Priya, Sam and Kevin played five too, so each loses their lowest result. Rosa played four and keeps all of them: 4 points either way. Played still shows every tournament a player played. Only the points change. The Tournaments list below is the same, all five still belong to the season. The season scrolled down: Standings 4 Tyler 21 pts, 5 Priya 19 pts, 6 Sam 8 pts, 7 Kevin 6 pts, 8 Rosa 4 pts. Tournaments: Sun, Nov 22, Dave won. Tue, Nov 17, Marcus won. Tue, Nov 10, Jenna won. Tue, Nov 3, Marcus won. Tue, Oct 27, Marcus won Pick a number a few below how many tournaments you expect in the season. If you play about twelve, 8 or 10 lets each player skip two to four nights. Dave picks 4 only because his season has five tournaments so far. He can raise it later, and the season recounts. Ties When two players have the same points: 1. The one with more wins goes first. 2. If wins are equal too, House Rules looks at each player's own latest tournament. The one who finished higher in theirs goes first. When the top two are tied on points, the headline says who leads on wins instead of a number of points. Share the standings Tap the share button at the top right of the season screen, the square with an arrow. Your phone's share sheet opens with 2026 Season, so you can send it to the club's group chat, a note or any other app. The share sheet over the season screen with 2026 Season at the top, then Reminders, More and Save to Files The text has the season's name, the club, the dates and each place with points, like 1. Marcus, 37 pts. It has no money. Season dates On the season screen, tap More and Season Dates. The season's More menu: Points Rules, Rename Season, Season Dates, End Season, Delete Season Starts: the first day of the season. Here Jan 1, 2026. Ends: turn it off for a season with no last day. Turn it on to pick the Last Day, here Dec 31, 2026. The note sums up the rule: Club tournaments that start in these dates and reach settlement score points. Tap the checkmark to save, or the X to close without changes. A shorter league, like a fall league from September to November, is just a season with those dates. Season Dates: Starts Jan 1, 2026, Ends on, Last Day Dec 31, 2026. Club tournaments that start in these dates and reach settlement score points To change the name, tap More and Rename Season. End a season When the league is over, tap More and End Season. House Rules asks first: End Season Today? Tournaments after today won't score points in this season. Tap End Season to confirm. There's no Cancel button: tap outside the box to cancel and keep the season running. End Season Today? Tournaments after today won't score points in this season. End Season button, coming from the More menu Ending a season sets today as its Last Day. Tournaments that start today still count, those that start later don't. The standings stay as they are, and you can still open the season. End Season is only in the menu while the season is running. Dave keeps his running. To start the next season, open the club, tap More and New Season, as in How Season Points Work. Delete a season More and Delete Season removes the season. House Rules asks first: Delete Season? Tournaments and their results stay. Only the season's standings go. Delete Season? Tournaments and their results stay. Only the season's standings go. Delete Season button in red Nothing is lost for good: the standings are counted from the tournaments, so a new season with the same dates and rules shows the same table again. Good to know Best Results Count works with both By Place and By Field. See How Season Points Work. A player who played fewer tournaments than the count keeps all their results. Changing Best Results Count, like any change in Points Rules, recounts the whole season at once. Related How Season Points Work Fixed Bounties and PKO Close Session, Step by Step

title: Blind Structures and Templates
headings: Build a template step by step
text: The Blind Timer runs a tournament's clock from a template. A template is a blind structure: the levels and breaks in order, with the blinds and the minutes of each. House Rules comes with three ready-made templates, builds your own step by step from a few answers, and lets you set every level by hand. This page shows the built-in templates, the step-by-step builder, and how to keep, copy and delete your own templates. Starting and running the clock is in Running the Timer. The example club All the screenshots come from the Maple Street Game. Dave is the host and also plays. He runs the club on his phone, so in this story you are Dave. The plan: ten players are coming for a long tournament. Everyone should start deep and have time to play, so Dave wants about five hours, 20,000 chips each and 20-minute levels. What happens: Dave looks at the built-in templates, builds his own one step by step, names it Maple Street Deep, and loads it into the timer. Open the Blind Timer In the Lobby, the app's home screen, tap Blind Timer. The screen lists the templates in two cards: Built-In: Standard, Turbo and Deep Stack. Each row shows the number of levels, the total time and the number of players it's made for. Standard has 12 levels, ≈ 3h 20m, 8 players. My Templates: the templates you made. It's empty at first. Blind Timer: Built-In with Standard 12 levels, about 3h 20m, 8 players, Turbo 11 levels, about 1h 55m, 6 players, Deep Stack 15 levels, about 5h 30m, 8 players. My Templates: No templates of your own yet. Build Step by Step and a plus button at the bottom At the bottom are two ways to make your own: Build Step by Step, where House Rules works out the levels from a few answers, and the + button, which opens a blank template to fill in by hand. Both are explained below. Look at a template Tap a template to see it. Dave opens Standard. The Structure card at the top sums it up: ≈ 3h 20m total time, 12 levels, 2 breaks, made for 8 players, a starting stack of 10,000 and a starting depth of 100 BB. The depth is the starting stack counted in big blinds: 10,000 chips at a big blind of 100. Standard: Structure, a balanced pace for a typical home tournament. About 3h 20m total time, 12 levels, 2 breaks, 8 players, 10,000 starting stack, 100 BB starting depth. Levels, 15 min levels: Level 1 50/100, Level 2 75/150, Level 3 100/200. Customize Copy and Use Template at the bottom Below it, Levels lists every level with its blinds and minutes, and the breaks between them. In Standard every level is 15 minutes: 12 levels of 15 minutes plus 2 breaks of 10 minutes make the 3h 20m. Blinds are written as small blind / big blind, so 50 / 100 is a small blind of 50 and a big blind of 100. From Level 5, the line under the blinds shows the ante, here ante 400 at 200 / 400. Standard scrolled down: Level 4 150/300, a 10 min break, Level 5 200/400 ante 400, Level 6 300/600 ante 600, up to Level 8, another 10 min break, then Level 9 1,000/2,000 ante 2,000 to Level 11 At the bottom: Use Template loads it into the timer. Customize Copy opens a copy to edit, named My Standard. The built-in templates themselves never change. Saving the copy puts it in My Templates. Build a template step by step The builder asks about your game in three short steps, works out the levels itself, and shows the result in a fourth step for you to check. Dave could almost use Deep Stack, but it runs about 5h 30m for 8 players, so he builds his own. On the Blind Timer screen, tap Build Step by Step. Dave sets Players to 10 and Playing Time to 5h, taps Continue, sets Starting Stack to 20,000, Depth to 200 BB and Level Length to 20 min, taps Continue, sets the ante from Level 6, taps Continue, and the Structure step shows 13 levels, 3 breaks, about 4h 50m, 200 BB The line at the top shows where you are, Step 1 of 4 to Step 4 of 4. Continue at the bottom goes to the next step, the arrow left of it goes back. Each step's card has a small i at its top right: tap it for a one-line explanation of the step. Step 1: Game The Tournament card starts with the Standard template's answers. Game, Step 1 of 4. Tournament: Players 8, Playing Time 3h 30m, Expected Re-entries 0. Continue at the bottom Players: how many start. Tap the number and type it on the keys that slide up. On the right are quick picks: 6, 8, 9 and 10 at the table. Tap the checkmark at the top right of the keys to keep it. Dave types 10. Playing Time: about how long the tournament should run, from 2h to 6h in half hours. Dave picks 5h. Expected Re-entries: how many re-entries you expect in all. Their chips are counted, and the late levels run longer. Dave expects none and leaves 0. The Players keys under the Game step: 10 typed, number keys, and quick picks 6, 8, 9 and 10 at the table The Playing Time menu: 2h, 2h 30m, 3h, 3h 30m checked, 4h, 4h 30m, 5h, 5h 30m, 6h Playing Time is a target, not an exact total: the builder fits whole levels into it, so the result can be a little shorter. The tournament may also end sooner, when one player has all the chips. Here the builder starts at 3h 30m even though Standard itself runs 3h 20m. Step 2: Stack and Pace Starting Stack: the chips each player gets. The keys offer 5,000, 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000. The line above the keys shows the Big blind at level 1 for the stack you type, at the depth set right now. Depth: the starting stack in big blinds: 100, 150, 200 or 250 BB. Deeper stacks give more room to play early on. Smallest Chip: the smallest chip on your table. The blinds are made of this chip, so every blind is one you can pay. 25 is the usual one. Level Length: the minutes of each level: 10, 12, 15, 20, 25 or 30. Longer levels make the pressure build more slowly. Starting Blinds: worked out from the stack and the depth. You don't set it. Dave types 20,000. The depth is still 100 BB from the Standard answers, so the keys show a first big blind of 200: 20,000 ÷ 100. The Starting Stack keys: 20,000 typed, Big blind at level 1 200, quick picks 5,000, 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000 chips Then he picks 200 BB for Depth, so the first big blind becomes 20,000 ÷ 200 = 100, and 20 min for Level Length. The Depth menu: 100 BB checked, 150 BB, 200 BB, 250 BB The card now shows Starting Blinds 50 / 100. Stack and Pace, Step 2 of 4: Starting Stack 20,000, Depth 200 BB, Smallest Chip 25, Level Length 20 min, Starting Blinds 50/100 If a choice can't make a smooth structure, a warning shows under the card and Continue stays off until you change it. Step 3: Ante and Breaks An ante is a small extra bet that goes into the pot before every hand, on top of the blinds. It makes the late levels move faster. Ante: No Ante, Ante from Each Player, where every player at the table pays it, or Big Blind Ante, where the player in the big blind pays one ante for the whole table, the size of the big blind. Ante From: the level the ante starts at, Level 2 to Level 12. It's hidden with No Ante. Breaks: No Breaks, or a break Every 2 levels up to Every 8 levels. Break Length: 5, 10, 15 or 20 min. It's hidden with No Breaks. The Ante menu: No Ante, Ante from Each Player, Big Blind Ante checked The Breaks menu: No Breaks, Every 2 levels to Every 8 levels, Every 4 levels checked Dave keeps Big Blind Ante and moves it to Level 6, so the first five levels run without an ante. He keeps a 10 min break Every 4 levels. Breaks count toward the total time. Ante and Breaks, Step 3 of 4: Ante Big Blind Ante, Ante From Level 6, Breaks Every 4 levels, Break Length 10 min Step 4: Structure The last step shows what the builder made. The Structure card sums it up: 13 levels, 3 breaks, ≈ 4h 50m total time and 200 BB starting depth. Structure, Step 4 of 4: 13 Levels, 3 Breaks, about 4h 50m Total Time, 200 BB Starting Depth, Fine-Tune Levels button. Levels: Level 1 50/100, Level 2 75/150, Level 3 125/250, Level 4 200/400, all 20 min. Save and Use at the bottom The total adds up from the levels: 13 levels of 20 minutes is 260 minutes, plus 3 breaks of 10 minutes, 290 minutes, or 4h 50m. It's a little under the 5 hours Dave asked for, because a structure only grows a whole level at a time. Levels lists every level with its blinds and minutes. From level 6 the ante follows in brackets: 400 / 800 (800) is a small blind of 400, a big blind of 800 and a big blind ante of 800. Breaks come after levels 4, 8 and 12, every four levels, so one more break falls just before the last level. The last level is 7,500 / 15,000. The Levels list: Level 3 125/250, Level 4 200/400, Break 10 min, Level 5 250/500, Level 6 400/800 (800), Level 7 500/1,000 (1,000), Level 8 1,000/2,000 (2,000), Break, Level 9 1,500/3,000 (3,000) to Level 12 5,000/10,000 (10,000), Break, Level 13 Fine-tune the levels To change a level yourself, tap Fine-Tune Levels. It opens the whole template for editing: its name, Players, Starting Stack, a Summary, and every level with its blinds and minutes in capsules. Tap a capsule to change it. Save keeps your changes, Cancel throws them away. Dave likes the levels as they are and taps Cancel. Fine-tune sheet My Home Tournament with Cancel and Save: Players 10, Starting Stack 20,000. Summary: Levels 13, Breaks 3, Total Time about 4h 50m, Starting Depth 200 BB. Levels with Edit: Level 1 50/100 20 min, Level 2 75/150 20 min If you fine-tune, then go back and change an answer in an earlier step, House Rules asks Rebuild Levels? before Continue builds the levels again, because your fine-tune edits will be lost. Save and use Tap Save and Use. A name box opens over the keyboard with My Home Tournament typed. Dave types Maple Street Deep and taps the checkmark. The X closes the box without saving. Dave taps Save and Use, types Maple Street Deep, taps the checkmark, and the timer opens at Level 1, 20:00, 50/100, Not started The name box over the Structure step: Maple Street Deep, an X on the left and a checkmark on the right The template is saved, and the timer opens with it: Level 1, 20:00 and 50 / 100, Not started. The clock doesn't run until you tap Start. Under the title, Maple Street Deep shows the 10 players it was built for. The timer with Maple Street Deep, 10 players: Level 1, 20:00, 50/100, Not started. Up Next: Level 2 75/150 20 min, Level 3 125/250 20 min. Start at the bottom To start the clock and run the evening, see Running the Timer. Pick another template Before you tap Start, you can still switch. Tap More, the three dots at the top right, then Change Template. Before Start there's nothing to lose, so the timer goes straight back to the list. Once the clock has started, House Rules asks first. The timer's More menu: Show Stacks, Change Template Your own templates Maple Street Deep is now in My Templates, with 13 levels, ≈ 4h 50m, 10 players. Tap it to look at it, change it with Edit, or load it with Use Template. Blind Timer with My Templates: Maple Street Deep, 13 levels, about 4h 50m, 10 players Touch and hold your template's row for two more actions: Duplicate makes a copy, so you can try a variation without losing the original. Delete removes it. House Rules asks first: Delete Template? "Maple Street Deep" will be deleted. This can't be undone. Tap Delete Template to confirm, or tap outside the box to keep it. The row menu over Maple Street Deep: Duplicate and Delete Delete Template? Maple Street Deep will be deleted. This can't be undone. Delete Template button in red, coming from the row Built-in templates have no such menu: they can't be deleted or changed. Make a template by hand If you already know your levels, for example from a printed blind sheet, tap the + button at the bottom of the Blind Timer screen. A New Template sheet opens: Template Name, then Players and Starting Stack. With a starting stack, the timer can show the average stack and the depth. Add adds a Level or a Break. Set the blinds and minutes with the capsules in the row. Swipe a level left to delete it. Tap Edit above the levels to reorder them. New Template with Cancel and Save: Template Name, Players 0, Starting Stack 0. Levels: Add. Add the first level. Set blinds and minutes with the capsules in the row The rules are the same for every template: the big blind is always twice the small blind, and the blinds must go up from level to level. Save at the top right keeps the template in My Templates. To start from a built-in template instead, open it and tap Customize Copy. Here is My Turbo, a copy of Turbo with all its levels, ready to change. My Turbo with Cancel and Save: Players 6, Starting Stack 5,000. Summary: Levels 11, Breaks 1, Total Time about 1h 55m, Starting Depth 100 BB. Levels: Level 1 25/50 10 min, Level 2 50/100 10 min Good to know Each template remembers the players and the starting stack it was made for. When it has a stack, the timer can show the average stack as players drop out. See Running the Timer. A club tournament runs its own timer from the blinds you chose when you set it up. See Setting Up a Tournament. Related Running the Timer Notifications and Lock Screen Setting Up a Tournament

title: Running the Timer
text: The Blind Timer keeps the clock for a tournament: how long the current level has left, the blinds now and the blinds coming next. It moves to the next level on its own, and you can pause it, skip a level or go back at any time. This page shows how to start the clock and run it through the evening. Choosing or building the blind structure is in Blind Structures and Templates. The example club All the screenshots come from the Maple Street Game. Dave is the host and also plays, so in this story you are Dave. The game: tonight's tournament is at Marcus's place. Marcus keeps the money, so Dave doesn't start a session for it in House Rules. He only uses the Blind Timer, and his Lobby has no sessions yet. The structure: the built-in Standard template: 8 players, 10,000 chips each, 15-minute levels. The blinds are the two forced bets that start each hand, written small blind / big blind: the first level is 50 / 100, a small blind of 50 and a big blind of 100. What happens: Dave starts the clock, pauses it for a phone call, jumps ahead to level 5, keeps track of who's out, and stops the timer at the end. Load a template In the Lobby, the app's home screen, tap Blind Timer. Tap a template, here Standard, and then Use Template at the bottom. The timer opens ready to go, but the clock doesn't run yet: Level 1, 15:00, 50 / 100, Not started. At the top is the template's name and the players it's made for, Standard, 8 players. Up Next shows what comes after this level, two rows, a break included when one is next. Standard, 8 players: Level 1, 15:00, 50/100, Not started. Up Next: Level 2 75/150 15 min, Level 3 100/200 15 min. Start at the bottom between two arrow buttons Start the clock Tap Start when the cards are in the air. The time counts down, and the bar under it fills as the level goes by. The first time you start a timer, your phone asks whether House Rules may send notifications. Tap Allow to get an alert when a level ends, even with the phone locked. If you tapped Don't Allow, the timer shows how to turn alerts on later. See Notifications and Lock Screen. The running timer: Level 1, 14:48, 50/100, a thin progress bar. Up Next Level 2 75/150 and Level 3 100/200. Pause at the bottom, Stop at the top right When the time runs out, the timer moves to the next level by itself and the new blinds show up. A break counts down the same way. The buttons Dave taps Pause at 14:43, the timer says Paused, he taps Resume, then the right arrow to Level 2 at 75/150, then the left arrow back to Level 1 There are always three buttons at the bottom: the left arrow, the big button in the middle (Start, then Pause or Resume), and the right arrow. At the top right are, from left to right, the list button for Levels, More (three dots) and Stop. Pause stops the clock, and the level card says Paused. Resume picks it up from the same second. Dave pauses at 14:43 for a phone call. The right arrow moves to the next level at once, with its full time. The left arrow goes back to the previous level. The paused timer: Level 1, 14:43 dimmed, 50/100, Paused. Resume at the bottom Level 2 after the right arrow: 14:59, 75/150. Up Next Level 3 100/200, Level 4 150/300 Jump to any level The list button at the top, left of the three dots, opens Levels: the whole structure with every level, its blinds, its minutes and the breaks. The current level is highlighted. Levels, Tap a level to jump to it: Level 1 50/100 highlighted, Level 2 75/150, Level 3 100/200, Level 4 150/300, Break 10 min, Level 5 200/400 ante 400, up to Level 11 2,000/4,000 ante 4,000, all 15 min While the clock is running or paused after Start, tap a level to jump to it. Before Start the rows can't be tapped. Dave's game started late at another table, so he moves to Level 5. A small box pops up from the row: Jump to Level 5? The level's clock starts from the top. Tap Jump, or tap outside the box to stay where you are. Jump to Level 5? The level's clock starts from the top. Jump button, coming from the Level 5 row The timer is now on Level 5 with 200 / 400 and a big blind ante 400: from this level the player in the big blind also puts in 400 more before each hand, one ante for everyone at the table, so nobody else has to pay one. Level 5, 15:00, 200/400, big blind ante 400. Up Next Level 6 300/600 ante 600, Level 7 500/1,000 ante 1,000 Restart a level If the clock ran while nobody was playing, for example during a long argument over a hand, start the current level again. Tap More, the three dots at the top right, then Restart Level. You can also touch and hold Pause. The timer's More menu: Restart Level, Show Stacks, Change Template House Rules asks: Restart Level? The current level's clock starts from the top. Tap Restart, or tap outside the box to keep the time as it is. Dave keeps it. Restart Level? The current level's clock starts from the top. Restart button in red Change Template in the same menu stops the timer and goes back to the list of templates. Once the clock has started, House Rules asks first. Keep track of the stacks The timer can show the average stack: how many chips the players still in have on average. That tells you how deep the game still is. Tap More and Show Stacks. With a template that has no starting stack, Stacks still counts players and entries and asks you to set the starting stack to see the average. Stacks: Average Stack 10,000, 25 BB at Level 5. 8 of 8 Players Left, 8 Entries, 80,000 Chips in Play, 10,000 Starting Stack. Player Out and Re-entry at the bottom Average Stack: all the chips in play divided by the players left. Under it, the same in big blinds at the current level: 10,000 is 25 BB at a big blind of 400. Players Left: 8 of 8 means 8 still in, out of 8 entries. Entries: every buy-in so far, re-entries included. Chips in Play: the starting stack times the entries, 80,000. Starting Stack: each entry's chips, from the template. If a count is off, tap Players Left, Entries or Starting Stack and type the right number on the keys that slide up. As the game goes on, tap the buttons at the bottom: Player Out when a player is knocked out. The chips stay in play, so the average goes up. Re-entry when a player who was out buys in again. It adds a player and a starting stack. Dave taps Player Out twice and Re-entry once. The average stack goes from 10,000 to 11,429, then 13,333, then 12,857, and a message at the bottom confirms each tap with Undo After one Player Out: Average Stack 11,429, 28 BB at Level 5, 7 of 8 Players Left, 8 Entries, 80,000 Chips in Play. A message at the bottom: Player Out, 7 of 8 left, Undo Sam is the first one out: 80,000 chips among 7 players is an average of 11,429. Then Kevin goes out: 80,000 among 6 is 13,333.
